stories.headline: Hoax bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe
stories.what_happened: A week of false bomb threats against passenger flights in Europe forced diversions and fighter-jet escorts. No explosives have been found.
stories.why_it_matters: Hoaxes cost little to send but strain airports, airlines and security services.

key_facts.fact: Dozens of commercial flights in Europe were targeted by false bomb threats during the week, forcing some planes to reroute and others to be escorted by fighter jets.
Nearly 30 passenger flights were targeted on Thursday, including flights bound for London, Madrid and Copenhagen.

On Friday, four flights bound for Madrid-Barajas were targeted, according to Spanish airport operator AENA; four aircraft flying over France were targeted and landed without incident, the French prime minister's office said.
No explosives have been found in any incident so far.

Hungary's defence minister said NATO scrambled jets three times within a few hours over threats to three passenger aircraft; Bulgaria's fighter jets escorted commercial aircraft after explosive alerts.
Ireland's government said threats to Irish media were likely part of a co-ordinated campaign of disruption; some staff at Irish media organisations were evacuated.
Some emails were signed by fighters of the Male State, a name matching a Russian group; AFP has not confirmed any link, and the group's founder denied involvement.
Experts say the hoaxes are hard to trace and cost the perpetrators almost nothing, but strain security services.
A Dublin-to-Rome Aer Lingus flight was forced by French jets to land at a military base at Evreux, about 100 kilometres west of Paris; Italian jets escorted a Finnair flight into Rome.
The EU transport chief said it was too early to say whether the Europe flight bomb threats are linked.

stories.geography: Ireland, France, Italy, Spain, Hungary, Bulgaria, Czech Republic

stories.headline: AI shares drive biggest US stock fall in more than a year
stories.what_happened: US stocks fell sharply on Thursday 5 November as investors worried the AI data-centre boom could slow after the midterm elections.
stories.why_it_matters: Share prices affect savings and pensions, and show how worried investors are about a big industry.

key_facts.fact: On Thursday the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5% into correction territory, the S&P 500 dropped about 4.4%, and the Dow lost roughly 1,833 points (3.4%).
The article describes these as the steepest one-day declines since the April 4, 2025 tariff shock.
The sell-off was rooted in fears about a slowdown in the buildout of artificial intelligence.
The Magnificent Seven group of big tech companies lost more than $1 trillion in aggregate market value; Nvidia led the losses, falling over 9%, a drop of more than $440 billion.
All 11 sectors of the S&P 500 finished lower.
Investors feared a Democratic-controlled Congress and state governments would tighten rules on AI and data centers; many people worry data centers will use up water and energy.
On Friday the Nasdaq bounced by 1.5% as some investors bought chip stocks, while Asian chip stocks fell sharply.

stories.headline: Paraguay's president faces impeachment after a bank collapses
stories.what_happened: Paraguay's president Santiago Peña said he would resign after Ueno Bank was shut down, but Congress did not accept it and impeachment moved ahead.
stories.why_it_matters: A bank failure can leave millions of people unable to reach their money.

key_facts.fact: Peña announced his resignation on Thursday, November 5, after Ueno Bank was shut down in the middle of the night because of a solvency crisis.
Congress did not accept the resignation; Peña remains formally in office while impeachment moves forward.
The collapse left about 3 million people without access to bank accounts.
The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings; the charges allege serious and systematic dereliction of duty linked to the bank.
Peña has denied wrongdoing; he formerly held a stake in Ueno's parent company and said he sold the shares in 2025.

stories.headline: Oil has its biggest weekly fall as Iran talks and fighting continue
stories.what_happened: Brent crude fell more than 16% over the week as investors weighed new US-Iran fighting against signs of a deal.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil makes fuel, so prices affect travel and the cost of goods.

key_facts.fact: Brent crude settled at about $98.32 on Friday and fell more than 16% for the week, while US crude lost nearly 13%.
Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, according to a Reuters report cited by CNBC.
Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally put the chance of fighting resuming at 80%.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it shot down a US drone over Qeshm Island and that tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz; the claims were not independently verified.
Trump spoke by phone with Qatar's emir, who stressed the need for diplomacy.

sources.title: Oil prices tumble for the week as investors weigh Iran conflict risk after midterm elections

stories.headline: Hundreds of thousands march in a nationwide strike in France
stories.what_happened: Unions and students marched across France on Thursday 5 November over pay and living costs.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how rising prices are pushing people onto the streets.

key_facts.fact: The nationwide day of action was on Thursday, 5 November 2026; Euronews reported about 600,000 marchers according to authorities and more than 1.5 million by union estimates.
The CGT union called for an immediate 10% minimum wage increase.
The protests grew out of a student movement that began in September over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu planned a social conference with employers and unions on the following Monday.

sources.title: Hundreds of thousands march in nationwide strike in France
